summary: Mobility is near normal with an MF-Index of 71 and strong fuel‑policy scores, but public transport ridership remains below pre‑pandemic levels and actual fuel savings are far short of the theoretical ceiling. High mobility scores in logistics, construction and retail pose economic and environmental risks that require targeted policy action.

signals.detail: The modelled ceiling of 35.7 million litres saved per week contrasts sharply with the measured 0.334 million litres in the first week of the mandate, indicating very low real‑world compliance despite a perfect fuel‑policy component score.

Daily PT trips total 1.24 million, yielding a ridership component of 72.7. This is still about 15 % below the 2025 recovery level and the 2019 baseline, suggesting modest recovery but insufficient to offset rising fuel consumption.

Logistics, construction and retail sectors show mobility scores above 90 and are classified as high risk, implying continued pressure on road networks, congestion and emissions while these sectors lag in WFH adoption.
WFH adoption varies widely—from 60 % in public/GLC jobs to under 10 % in logistics, construction and retail—creating unequal exposure to fuel costs and commuting burdens across the workforce.
High RON95 price (RM4.27/L) could incentivise a shift to mass transit, yet ridership growth is modest and high‑risk sectors remain car‑dependent, limiting the expected modal shift.

recommendation: Introduce tiered WFH incentives for logistics, construction and retail to raise sectoral adoption to at least 30 % within six months, and complement this with targeted fuel‑efficiency subsidies for commercial fleets. Simultaneously, boost PT service frequency and fare discounts in high‑traffic corridors to accelerate ridership recovery and reduce reliance on private vehicles.
